question: Q15

prior_assessment.note: Smyth §2914 (with b: after a preposition + anarthrous noun δέ 'usually takes the third place') and §2916 checked on Alpheios. The quotation 'may often come third ... and even fourth' comes from §2916, which is explicitly about POETRY; the reference leaves this out. The 'δέ in seventh position' argument also holds only if δέ is a connective. Under c, δέ would be apodotic (Smyth §2837; KG II.2 §532) and would stand second in its own clause. So position alone does not exclude c.

Theon p. 56 Hiller table (ἡμιτόνιον ἡμιτόνιον τριημιτόνιον / χρωματικόν) confirmed in the Hiller transcription (First1KGreek tlg1724). It shows that the phrase describes the whole tetrachord, which is against reading it with τριημιτόνιον (b). It does not decide between a and c. The relevant Theon material is pp. 54-55 (see new findings).

Text verified (Jan p. 262, Meibom p. 26, Jan OCR and First1KGreek): '... εἶτα ἐπὶ τούτοις ἀσύνθετον τριημιτόνιον. ἵνα καὶ τοῦτο, εἰ καὶ μὴ ἐκ δύο τόνων καὶ ἡμιτονίου ἄντικρύς ἐστιν ...'. A remark about the whole tetrachord follows the naming of the trihemitone and shifts its subject. This is a modest parallel for a's appended summary colon, not proof.

Smyth §2772 checked (δέ is postpositive). §2914b says δέ 'usually' takes the third place after a preposition + anarthrous noun, not 'only'; §2914a allows exceptions for emphasis. The same objection applies: under c, δέ is apodotic, so its distance from the start of the participial phrase is irrelevant.

The Cleonides facts are confirmed in the Greek (Jan p. 181: ἐπὶ δὲ τὸ ὀξὺ ἐναντίως κατὰ ἡμιτόνιον καὶ ἡμιτόνιον καὶ τριημιτόνιον; p. 188: τὸ τριημιτόνιον ἐν μὲν χρώματι ἀσύνθετον). This shows the whole-tetrachord sense and so tells against b. It does not choose between a and c.
Facts verified as for Q15-05. The inference 'supports c' does not follow: reference to the whole fourth fits a (a closing colon with an implied subject, cf. Smyth §943) just as well.

Smyth §2837 verified verbatim: apodotic δέ is 'infrequent in Attic prose, where it is used especially after an emphatic personal or demonstrative pronoun or when a participle represents the antecedent clause'. Confirmed by KG II.2 §532 Anm. p. 277. Caveat: in the examples of both grammars, δέ follows a contrasted or resumptive word and often has concessive force ('obgleich ... doch'). This makes c possible, not likely.
Smyth §943 verified: the subject may shift without warning when there is no danger of obscurity (T. 7.25; D. 59.115). This supports a's implicit subject (the whole tetrachord).
Smyth §§944-945, 948 verified (omission of the copula and of a verb easily supplied). Only of general relevance.
Smyth §§2054-2056 verified. A circumstantial participle agreeing with the subject is normal; that makes c grammatical but does not choose between the options.
The Cleonides facts are correct (Jan pp. 181, 187-188). The reference rightly says that a and b need either a shift of subject or a loose construction.
Smyth §2914 verified. Its bearing is slight: εἴη δ’ more naturally opens a new clause.
Jan p. 181 verified in the First1KGreek transcription (the text has χρῶμα and τριημιτόνιον). This is against b; it does not choose between a and c.
Jan p. 188 verified: τὸ τριημιτόνιον ἐν μὲν χρώματι ἀσύνθετον, ἐν δὲ διατόνῳ σύνθετον. This confirms τριημιτόνιον ἀσύνθετον as the single remaining step.

Smyth §§2054-2056 verified. The Thuc. 1.29 example (προπέμψαντες κήρυκα πόλεμον προεροῦντα) illustrates agreement of a participle with the subject. It says nothing about a fronted participle followed by a clause with δέ, which is what c needs.

CGCG §1.9 n.1 and §1.13 verified in the publisher's preview (pageplace.de). They concern modern punctuation of ANCIENT texts, and §1.13 itself says punctuation was introduced in Byzantine times. For an author of 1008 transmitted in a manuscript of 1040, Byzantinist guidance (Giannouli 2014) is that the punctuation of reliable witnesses should be taken into account. The principle permits repunctuation but does not favour c.
This duplicates Q15-07. Grammatically correct: δέ's position does not by itself force a stop before εἴη. Same caveats on frequency, register and pattern.

new_findings.source: Theon Smyrnaeus, Expositio, ed. Hiller (1878) pp. 54.1-55.7. Page image of p. 55 (archive.org theonissmyrnaei00theogoog, leaf n76) and the First1KGreek transcription tlg1724.tlg001
new_findings.found: This is the author's model, with many verbal echoes. Theon p. 54.11: διὰ τῶν τόνων τὸ πλεῖστον; p. 55.15-17: διὰ τὸ εἶναι ἄριστον, ἀπενεγκάμενον ... τὴν προσηγορίαν; p. 56: the δυσμελῳδητότατον ... Πλάτων sentence, reproduced at Bas. 33. On the chromatic, Theon writes: '... οὔτε διάστημα δύναται ποιήσασθαι ἄλλο πλὴν τὸ λειπόμενον ..., τὸ τριημιτονιαῖον ἀσύνθετον, ... · ὥστε γίνεσθαι τὴν τοιαύτην μελῳδίαν κατὰ ἡμιτόνιον καὶ ἡμιτόνιον καὶ τριημιτόνιον ἀσύνθετον. καλεῖται δὲ πάλιν τὸ γένος τῆς τοιαύτης μελῳδίας χρωματικὸν διὰ τὸ ... τοῦ πρόσθεν γοερώτερόν τε καὶ παθητικώτερον ἦθος ἐμφαίνειν.' In the source, the composition of the whole tetrachord closes the period about the remainder (a ὥστε-clause whose subject shifts to the whole). The naming begins a new sentence with connective δέ (καλεῖται δέ), and that sentence is the counterpart of 'εἴη δ’ ἂν τοῦτο ... χρωματικόν, παθητικώτερόν τε τοῦ προτέρου καὶ γοερώτερον'. For the diatonic, Theon puts the composition after the name (καλεῖται δὲ τὸ οὕτω μελῳδηθὲν σύστημα τετράχορδον, συνεστηκὸς ἐκ ... ἡμιτονίου καὶ τόνου καὶ τόνου), exactly as the author does at Bas. 32.7-9.
new_findings.bears_on: a (against c; against b as to sense)
new_findings.how: The author keeps Theon's order in both genera. The chromatic composition corresponds to Theon's ὥστε-clause, which ends the preceding period. εἴη δ’ corresponds to καλεῖται δέ, a sentence-initial connective δέ, not an apodotic one. This supports the witnesses' stop before εἴη. Hiller's high point before ὥστε is editorial, but it matches a's high point better than b's comma.

new_findings.source: Theon, ed. Hiller p. 55, apparatus to line 4: a marginal note in Theon's cod. A
new_findings.found: At τριημιτόνιον ἀσύνθετον, cod. A has in the margin: 'τὸ τριημιτόνιον τριῶν ἐστὶν ἡμιτονίων, τόνου α ς· εἶτα τὰ β ἡμιτόνια· γίνεται ἡ πᾶσα τόνων β ς'. This is a Byzantine reader's computation of the whole tetrachord (two semitones + trihemitone = 2½ tones), attached to the naming of the incomposite trihemitone.
new_findings.how: This is a weak parallel. A Byzantine reader placed the summary of the whole tetrachord's composition exactly where the author has ἐξ ἡμιτονίων δύο καὶ τριημιτονίου συγκεκραμένον, as an appendix to 'τριημιτόνιον ἀσύνθετον', with its own (implied) subject 'the whole'. This fits a construal of the participle as a closing colon of the preceding sentence.

new_findings.source: Kühner–Gerth, Ausführliche Grammatik II.2 (1904) §532 'Δέ im Nachsatze', pp. 275-277, esp. p. 277 Anmerk. (page image, archive.org p2ausfhrlichegra02khuoft, leaf n292)
new_findings.found: Apodotic δέ is chiefly Homeric and fairly frequent in Herodotus, rarer in Attic prose. There it is 'häufig in Verbindung mit einem Personal- oder Demonstrativpronomen' contrasted with a word of the antecedent clause. Anmerk.: 'So steht δέ, besonders bei den Attikern, auch hinter verkürzten Vordersätzen in der Form des Partizips.' Examples: X. Mem. 3.7.8 (χειρούμενος, τούτοις δὲ ..., glossed 'obgleich .. doch'); X. An. 6.6.16 (οἰόμενοι ... τιμῆς τεύξεσθαι, ἀντὶ δὲ τούτων ...); Hell. 3.3.7; Pl. Symp. 220b (genitive absolute ..., οὗτος δ’ ...); Hdt. 5.50; Antiph. 1.12, 2.β.4; Isocr. 15.71.
new_findings.how: This confirms that c's construction (a participial antecedent, then a main clause with apodotic δέ) is real Greek. In every example, though, δέ attaches to a word contrasted with or resuming the participial clause, mostly with concessive or adversative force. In c, δέ would follow the verb εἴη and mark no contrast, so the match is imperfect.

new_findings.found: Smyth's prose examples of apodotic δέ with participles are T. 1.11 (ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἀφικόμενοι μάχῃ ἐκράτησαν ..., φαίνονται δ’ οὐδ’ ἐνταῦθα ...: a finite ἐπειδή-clause containing a participle, with δέ after the verb) and P. S. 220b (a genitive absolute, then οὗτος δ’ ...). There is no example of a bare circumstantial participle agreeing with the main subject and followed by verb + δέ.
new_findings.how: Apodotic δέ after a verb is attested (T. 1.11), so c is not impossible. The closest exact pattern (an agreeing participle + verb δ’ ἄν + resumptive demonstrative) is not illustrated.

new_findings.source: The author's own syntax: Bas. lines and P passages in pkg/evidence (sections 1-7)
new_findings.found: In every place where a preposed antecedent is followed by its main clause, the main clause has NO apodotic δέ. Participial phrase: Bas. 23.8-9 (γινόμενον, καλῶς ἄν ποτε γένοιτο). Genitive absolute: Bas. 24.8-14 (ἧς ... θεωρουμένης, ἐν ἐπιτόμῳ διαληψόμεθα); Bas. 32.5-6 (δύο τονιαίων διαστημάτων ἐκτιθεμένων, ἀνάγκη). Participle agreeing with the subject: Bas. 26.24-27.1 (μεταλαβὼν ... περιθεὶς, ἥμισυ ... ποιεῖ); Bas. 27.1-2 (μετειληφὼς ..., τὸ δοθὲν διπλασιάζει); Bas. 30.2-6 (ἔχον, ... φαίνεται ἡμιόλιος). εἰ-clauses: Bas. 24.23; 31.18-24; 32.9-10; 32.15-16. P, Vinc. 338.4-7: Εἰ γὰρ ..., ἐντεῦθεν ἐγγίνεται. In the text, δέ after a verb plus ἄν is always a sentence-initial connective: τάχα δ’ ἄν τις (Bas. 24.4); τῇ γεωμετρίᾳ δέ (Bas. 26.22).
new_findings.how: Under c, Bas. 32.13 would be this author's only apodotic δέ. His regular practice is to front a participle and then give the main clause without a particle.

new_findings.source: Punctuation practice of H (Pal. gr. 281, AD 1040) and V in this text, from pkg/evidence
new_findings.found: H marks the boundary between a preposed antecedent and its main clause with ',' or '.', never with '·', in every case examined: H 64r.6 γινόμενον, κα|λῶς; 64r.22 χαριζο|μένης, περὶ; 64v.11 ἐκφωνηθείη, ἀπη|χής; 65r.7 ἀναφαίνεται, τὸν αὐτόν; 65v.13-14 ὄν|τα. οὔτε; 66r.1 περιθεὶς. ἥμισυ (the '·' at 65v.22 μεταλαβὼν· stands between two coordinated participles inside the antecedent); 66r.3 πλευρὰν, τὸ δο|θέν; 68v.20 προάγοι|το. τὸ διάτονον; 68v.21 ἡμιτονίων, τό; 69r.1 συνέχεται, τό; 69r.9 ἐντι|θεμένων. ἀνάγκη; 69r.13 ἡμιτόνια. τό; 69r.21 προά|γοιτο. θάτερον. After συγκεκραμένον, H has '·', its stronger stop, the one it uses at the end of a colon or period. V marks antecedent/main boundaries with ',' (81r.18, 81r.20, 81v.1, 81v.10, 82r.3), though once with '·' (77v.3 ὄντα· οὔτε). After συγκεκραμένον, V has its strongest sign ':' (used elsewhere at sentence ends, e.g. 81r.21, 81v.15, 82r.6, 82r.8), and εἴη carries a red initial at the start of line 81v.20, while 81v.19 (καί) has none.
new_findings.how: The oldest witness, written 32 years after the work, punctuates as if the period ended at συγκεκραμένον. If H's scribe had taken the participle as the antecedent of εἴη, his habit would have been ',' or '.' there. All four witnesses agree on a stop there. This is evidence of near-contemporary reading, not of the author's own pointing.

new_findings.source: A. Giannouli, 'Byzantine punctuation and orthography. Between normalisation and respect of the manuscripts', COMSt Newsletter 8 (2014) 18-22 (open access, CC BY), §1
new_findings.found: Dionysius Thrax distinguishes upper, middle and low dots; the upper and low dots relate to the (in)completeness of a thought. Studies of practice from the 9th to the 12th century show 'that, in principle, the scribes followed the theoretical guidelines of the grammarians'. Transmitted punctuation 'marks the cola' and helps avoid misinterpretation. 'Especially in the case of post ninth-century Byzantine authors the transmitted punctuation should be taken into account by modern editors ... Variations, especially with regard to the strong pauses, are less than some editors would think.' Transmitted punctuation 'shows how ancient editors understood the text'.
new_findings.how: This gives methodological weight to the unanimous strong pause after συγκεκραμένον in H (1040) and the other witnesses. Byzantine punctuation is partly rhythmic, though: H also has '.' between τοῦτο and τὸ διὰ τεσσάρων. So it guides the editor but does not bind him.

new_findings.source: Bacchius, Isagoge §23 (Jan, MSG p. 298); Gaudentius, Isagoge 5 (Jan p. 331, Meibom p. 6); Cleonides 3 (Jan p. 181); Nicomachus, Ench. 12 (Jan p. 262). Jan OCR on archive.org (musiciscriptoresjank) and First1KGreek
new_findings.found: Every theorist states the chromatic composition in a sentence of its own, with κατὰ ἡμιτόνιον καὶ ἡμιτόνιον καὶ τριημιτόνιον (Bacchius: 'Τὸ δὲ χρῶμα πῶς μελῳδεῖται; — Ἐπὶ μὲν τὸ ὀξὺ καθ’ ἡμιτόνιον καὶ ἡμιτόνιον καὶ τριημιτόνιον'; Gaudentius: 'τὸ δὲ χρωματικὸν ... καθ’ ἡμιτόνιον καὶ ἡμιτόνιον καὶ τριημιτόνιον') or as a list (Nicomachus). None uses a participle such as συγκεκραμένον/συγκείμενον ἐξ ... for the chromatic tetrachord.
new_findings.how: There is no formulaic model that would favour attaching the participial phrase to the naming sentence (c) or to the preceding sentence (a/b). The participle is the author's own addition.

new_findings.source: Vincent, Notices et extraits 16.2, p. 340 (P passage, in pkg/evidence section-4)
new_findings.found: The author's (or P's) vocabulary uses κεράννυμι for the fusion of several intervals into one incomposite interval: 'τῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς κεκραμένων διαστημάτων ... οὕτως εἰς ἓν διάστημα ὡς ἐξ φθάρσεως κίρνανται'. Compare Bas. 27.6-8, ὡς ἓν ἐκ συμφθάρσεως διὰ ... τριῶν ἡμιτονίων.
new_findings.how: συγκεκραμένον belongs to the author's vocabulary of σύμφθαρσις, which might tempt a reader to construe it with τριημιτόνιον ἀσύνθετον (b). The ingredients named (two semitones AND a trihemitone) make that construal impossible, so the lexical point does not rescue b.

searched_without_result:
1. Denniston, The Greek Particles, on apodotic δέ after a participle: no legitimate access. The Internet Archive lending copies (greekparticles0000jdde, greekparticles0000jdde_l4p5) are restricted and their search-inside endpoint returned 'Item not available'. Google Books shows no preview for any Denniston edition. HathiTrust returned a Cloudflare bot challenge, which I did not bypass. A freely downloadable but apparently unauthorized full scan on archive.org (folkscanomy collection) was deliberately not used.
2. Apodotic δέ after a participial antecedent in technical prose. I ran a mechanical scan of Theon (Hiller), Nicomachus (Arith. and Ench.), Aristoxenus (Harm.) and Cleonides (First1KGreek) for ', X δέ' following participle-bearing clauses without μέν. No clear apodotic instance turned up; all hits were coordinative or μέν-less contrastive δέ. No 'εἴη δ’' occurs at all in these texts. In Theon, 'ἂν εἴη' after a genitive absolute appears without δέ (Hiller p. 121: ... ἴσον ἀπεχόντων τὸ σχῆμα ἂν εἴη σφαιρικόν). Ptolemy (Düring), Proclus, Porphyry's commentary and Byzantine scholia were not available in the corpora I could reach.
3. Byzantine punctuation handbooks (Noret, Byzantion 65, 1995; Reinsch, 'Stixis und Hören'; the Giannouli–Schiffer 2011 volume; Gaffuri): not accessible online. Only Giannouli 2014 was read.
4. The open-access Études Classiques 89 (2021) 5-50 article on δέ in post-classical documentary texts: seen only through a search abstract, which reports apodotic δέ after preposed subordinate clauses in papyri. The page returned 403, so the article was not used as evidence.
5. The CGCG section on apodotic δέ: not consulted; only the publisher's preview is legitimately available.
6. No theorist found who describes the chromatic tetrachord with ἐξ + genitives + a participle.
decisive: Nothing decisive. Option c is admissible Greek: apodotic δέ after a participial antecedent is attested in Attic and Herodotean prose (KG II.2 §532 Anm. p. 277; Smyth §2837). Punctuation is editorial, and H's stops record a scribe's reading, not the author's. Against c, three independent and convergent lines of evidence point to a: (1) the author's model sentence in Theon pp. 54-55, where the naming sentence begins with connective καλεῖται δέ; (2) the author's consistent avoidance of apodotic δέ; (3) the strong stop in all witnesses, including H of 1040, whose lighter signs mark antecedent/main boundaries elsewhere. Against b, the sense rules it out, because the participle cannot qualify τριημιτόνιον. None of this is conclusive.
reasoning:
The three options differ on where the sentence boundary falls and what ἐξ ἡμιτονίων δύο καὶ τριημιτονίου συγκεκραμένον qualifies. The theorists (Theon's table, Cleonides, Nicomachus, Bacchius, Gaudentius) all make clear that two semitones + a trihemitone is the whole chromatic tetrachord. The participle therefore cannot qualify τριημιτόνιον, which b's comma suggests. a and c both refer it to the whole. c gives it a grammatical head (τοῦτο τὸ διὰ τεσσάρων γένος) but needs εἴη δ’ to be an apodotic δέ. a keeps it as a closing colon with an implied subject (Smyth §943).

Grammar allows c. KG II.2 §532 Anm. and Smyth §2837 attest apodotic δέ after participial antecedents, so the prior 'δέ in seventh position' argument (Q15-01, Q15-04) is misframed. But the attested pattern has δέ after a contrasted or resumptive word, usually with concessive force, which is not the situation here.

Three findings tip the balance to a. (i) The model is Theon pp. 54-55, closely echoed throughout the section. Theon ends the remainder-sentence with a ὥστε-clause giving the whole composition, then begins a new sentence 'καλεῖται δὲ πάλιν τὸ γένος ... χρωματικὸν ... γοερώτερόν τε καὶ παθητικώτερον'. That sentence corresponds to 'εἴη δ’ ἂν τοῦτο ... χρωματικόν, παθητικώτερόν τε ... καὶ γοέτερον', whose δέ is the same sentence-initial connective. The author's participle sits where Theon's ὥστε-clause sits, and where a Byzantine marginal note in Theon's cod. A sums the whole. (ii) The author never uses apodotic δέ in about a dozen comparable antecedent/main structures. (iii) H (1040) punctuates antecedent/main boundaries with ',' or '.' but puts its strong '·' after συγκεκραμένον. V has its strongest ':' and a red initial at εἴη, and all witnesses stop there. Byzantinist guidance (Giannouli 2014) gives such transmitted strong pauses weight.

Among the strong-stop options, a's high point after ἀσύνθετον better signals that the participle does not qualify the trihemitone; it matches H and V and the colon structure of Theon. Hence a, with moderate strength. The main counterweight is c's grammatical neatness, together with the fact that apodotic δέ after participles is attested.
seen_prohibited: Hiller's apparatus to Theon p. 55 (line 2) cites Bryennius (p. 397) for a variant reading in Theon; I saw it on the page image and did not use it. Jan's apparatus in the Musici scriptores OCR may cite later Byzantine writers; I did not use any such citation. None of the sources I opened (Smyth, Kühner–Gerth, Giannouli, CGCG preview, Theon/Hiller, Nicomachus, Cleonides, Bacchius, Gaudentius, Aristoxenus, Euclid, the Prais thesis) quoted or discussed the anonymous Quadrivium of 1008, Heiberg's edition, 'Anon. Quadr.' or 'Ps.-Psellus'. I used Vincent only through the pkg evidence file. No Greek phrase of the text was put into a search engine.
